subtopic: India and Brazil — A Comparative Overview
stem: Complete the sentence by choosing the appropriate alternative : India and Brazil have ____ type of government.
solution: India and Brazil have a Republic type of government. Both countries are federal democratic republics with a written constitution and an elected head of state — India is a parliamentary republic headed by a President, while Brazil is a presidential republic. 'Republic' is the description that is true of BOTH countries; 'Presidential' fits only Brazil, since India follows the parliamentary system.

stem: Complete the sentence by choosing the appropriate alternative : The Himalayas block the ____ winds blowing from the north.
solution: The Himalayas block the very cold winds blowing from the north. The lofty Himalayan wall stops the icy cold winds coming from Central Asia and Siberia from entering the Indian subcontinent. Because of this barrier, northern India stays much warmer in winter than places at the same latitude on the other side of the mountains.

stem: Complete the sentence by choosing the appropriate alternative : The economy of Brazil is mainly dependent on the ____ activities.
solution: The economy of Brazil is mainly dependent on tertiary activities. Services (trade, transport, banking, tourism, administration) contribute about 67% of Brazil's GDP and employ about 71% of its working population — far more than the primary and secondary sectors. This is confirmed by the pie diagrams printed in Q.6(B) of this very paper.

stem: Complete the sentence by choosing the appropriate alternative : Areawise Brazil ranks ____ in the world.
solution: Areawise Brazil ranks fifth in the world. With an area of about 85.16 lakh sq km it comes after Russia, Canada, China and the U.S.A. It is the largest country of South America, occupying nearly half of the continent. (India, by comparison, ranks seventh with about 32.87 lakh sq km.)

subtopic: Purpose and Planning of a Field Visit
stem: Find the odd man out : Materials to be carried for a field visit.
solution: Computer is the odd one out. A questionnaire, a camera and a note-book are light, portable materials that are actually carried into the field to collect and record information on the spot. A computer is a bulky instrument used later, back at the study centre, to tabulate and analyse the collected data — it is not carried on a field visit.

stem: Find the odd man out : Rivers in Brazil.
solution: Ganga is the odd one out. The Amazon, the Paraguay and the Uruguay are all rivers of Brazil — the Amazon drains the northern lowland, while the Paraguay and the Uruguay rise in the Brazilian Highlands and drain southwards into the Plata system. The Ganga is a river of India, rising in the Himalayas and flowing into the Bay of Bengal.

stem: Find the odd man out : Primary activities.
solution: Tourism is the odd one out. Agriculture, mining and fishing are primary activities — in each of them wealth is obtained directly from nature. Tourism is a tertiary (service) activity: it produces no goods but provides services such as travel, lodging and guidance.

stem: Find the odd man out : Favourable factors for concentration of settlements.
solution: Unfavourable climate is the odd one out. Availability of water, fertile land and a favourable climate all attract people and lead to dense, concentrated settlements. An unfavourable climate (extreme cold, extreme heat or very low rainfall) drives people away and results in sparse and scattered settlement.

context: State whether the following sentences are right or wrong (any four).
stem: The proportion of youth in India's population is high.
solution: Right. India has a young age structure — a large share of its people fall in the 15 to 59 working-age group, and the median age is only about 28 years. High birth rates in the recent past have widened the base of the age-sex pyramid, so the proportion of youth is high. This large youthful population is described as India's 'demographic dividend'.

context: State whether the following sentences are right or wrong (any four).
stem: India and Brazil have the same seasons at the same time.
solution: Wrong. India lies wholly in the Northern Hemisphere while the greater part of Brazil lies in the Southern Hemisphere. Because the two hemispheres are tilted towards the Sun at opposite times of the year, their seasons are reversed — when it is summer in India (June) it is winter in Brazil, and when India has winter (December) Brazil has summer. Hence the two countries do NOT have the same seasons at the same time.

context: State whether the following sentences are right or wrong (any four).
stem: Manaus is a port on the confluence of Negro and the Amazon.
solution: Right. Manaus, the chief city of the state of Amazonas in northern Brazil, stands where the dark-watered Rio Negro joins the muddy Solimoes (Amazon). It is a major inland river port about 1,500 km from the Atlantic, reached even by ocean-going ships because the Amazon is deep and navigable. The meeting of the two differently-coloured waters here is famous as the 'Meeting of the Waters'.

subtopic: Sex Ratio, Literacy and Life Expectancy
context: State whether the following sentences are right or wrong (any four).
stem: The sex ratio is high in Brazil.
solution: Right. Brazil has a favourable sex ratio — there are slightly more than 1,000 females for every 1,000 males (about 1,025 females per 1,000 males), so females actually outnumber males. This is much higher than India's sex ratio of about 943 females per 1,000 males. The higher female life expectancy and the absence of a strong preference for male children keep Brazil's sex ratio high.

context: State whether the following sentences are right or wrong (any four).
stem: Brazil is the only country in the world where both tigers and lions are found.
solution: Wrong. It is INDIA, not Brazil, that is the only country in the world where both tigers and lions are found in the wild — the Royal Bengal tiger in reserves such as Sundarbans, Corbett and Tadoba, and the Asiatic lion in the Gir forest of Gujarat. Brazil has neither; its largest wild cat is the jaguar of the Amazon rainforest.

context: Give geographical reasons for the following (any two).
stem: Most of the Himalayan rivers are perennial in nature.
solution: The Himalayan rivers such as the Ganga, the Yamuna, the Brahmaputra and the Indus rise in the snow-covered and glaciated higher Himalayas. They therefore receive water from two independent sources : (i) the monsoon rainfall from June to September, and (ii) the steady melting of snow and glacier ice during the hot summer months when there is no rain. Because one source takes over exactly when the other fails, these rivers carry water throughout the year and are perennial. Peninsular rivers, in contrast, depend only on rain and dry up in summer.

context: Give geographical reasons for the following (any two).
stem: Tropical cyclones occur rarely in Brazil.
solution: A tropical cyclone needs sea-surface temperatures above about \(27^\circ\)C, a low vertical wind shear and a sufficient Coriolis force. Off the coast of Brazil in the South Atlantic none of these is properly satisfied — the cold Falkland (Malvinas) current and the general cooling of the South Atlantic keep the sea surface too cool, strong upper-level westerlies create high wind shear that tears developing storms apart, and the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone rarely shifts far enough south of the Equator for cyclones to form. Moreover, near the Equator the Coriolis force is almost zero, so the winds cannot acquire the necessary rotation. Hence tropical cyclones occur rarely in Brazil.

context: Give geographical reasons for the following (any two).
stem: Settlements are sparse in North-Eastern Brazil.
solution: The interior of north-eastern Brazil (the sertao) has a semi-arid climate with scanty and highly uncertain rainfall, and it suffers frequent and prolonged droughts. The natural vegetation is the thorny Caatinga scrub, the soils are poor and there is a severe shortage of surface water and irrigation. Agriculture is therefore risky, industries and employment are few, and people migrate out of the region to the industrial south-east. All these unfavourable conditions keep the density of population low, so settlements in north-eastern Brazil are sparse and scattered.

context: Give geographical reasons for the following (any two).
stem: The waterways are not developed in Brazil.
solution: Although Brazil has huge rivers, its inland waterways are poorly developed. The Amazon, its largest navigable river, flows through the thinly-populated equatorial rainforest where there is little trade to carry, while the densely-populated and industrial south-east is drained by highland rivers such as the Sao Francisco and the Parana which are full of rapids and waterfalls and are therefore not navigable. The rivers also flow away from, rather than towards, the main markets, and the dense forest makes the building of river ports and terminals costly. Consequently roadways and airways have been developed instead, and waterways remain undeveloped.

subtopic: Purpose and Planning of a Field Visit
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two).
stem: What is field visit? What preparations should be done before going to a field visit?
solution:
A field visit is a planned visit to an actual site or region in order to observe geographical facts at first hand, to collect primary information and to verify what has been learnt from books and maps. It turns the field itself into a laboratory, so the knowledge gained is direct, accurate and permanent.

Preparations to be made before a field visit :
1. Decide the objective — fix clearly what is to be studied (e.g. a river, a market, a factory, a village).
2. Select the place and the season, and study it beforehand from maps, books, statistics and the internet.
3. Take permission from the school and, if necessary, from the authorities of the place to be visited, and inform parents.
4. Plan the journey — route, means of transport, timing, expenditure, stay and food.
5. Prepare a questionnaire and decide how the observations will be recorded.
6. Carry the necessary materials — note-book, pen and pencil, questionnaire, map of the area, camera, measuring tape, compass, water bottle, first-aid kit and identity card.
7. Divide the students into groups and give each group a definite responsibility.
8. Note the safety rules and behaviour to be followed at the site.

subtopic: Types of Economy and National Income
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two).
stem: What problems did Brazil and India face after Independence?
solution:
Both India (independent 1947) and Brazil (independent 1822) had been colonies, and after independence both faced very similar problems :
1. Poverty and inequality — a large section of the people lived below the poverty line, and income was very unequally distributed between a rich minority and a poor majority.
2. Illiteracy — literacy rates were low, and educational facilities were few, especially in rural areas.
3. Over-dependence on agriculture and on the export of a few raw materials — India on food crops and Brazil on coffee — which made the economy unstable.
4. Lack of industries, capital and technology, so raw materials had to be exported and finished goods imported.
5. Poorly developed transport and communication, and a shortage of power supply.
6. Rapid growth of population, unemployment and under-employment.
7. Large-scale migration from villages to cities, causing the growth of slums (favelas in Brazil).
8. Regional imbalance in development — the north-east of Brazil and the eastern and central parts of India lagged far behind the developed regions.
9. Malnutrition, poor health services and a high infant mortality rate.

Both countries therefore adopted planned development, land reforms, industrialisation and the spread of education to overcome these problems.

context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two).
stem: What environmental issues are faced by Brazil and India?
solution:
Environmental issues faced by Brazil and India :
1. Deforestation — in Brazil the Amazon rainforest, the 'lungs of the world', is being cleared for ranching, soyabean farming, mining, roads and dams; in India forests are cleared for agriculture, settlement, industry and development projects. This causes loss of the carbon sink and increases global warming.
2. Loss of biodiversity — destruction of habitat is endangering wildlife such as the jaguar and the macaw in Brazil and the tiger, the one-horned rhinoceros and the Asiatic lion in India.
3. Soil erosion and land degradation — heavy rain on cleared slopes, over-grazing and faulty farming remove the topsoil; the semi-arid north-east of Brazil and parts of Rajasthan and Maharashtra face desertification.
4. Water pollution — untreated sewage, industrial effluents and mining waste (mercury from gold-mining in the Amazon) pollute the rivers; in India the Ganga, the Yamuna and the Godavari are badly polluted.
5. Air pollution and smog in the large industrial cities — Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil; Delhi, Mumbai and Kolkata in India — from vehicles and industries.
6. Unplanned urbanisation — slums (favelas) and shanty towns without sanitation, and the growing problem of solid-waste disposal.
7. Displacement of tribal and indigenous people by large dams and mining projects.
8. Climate change effects — irregular rainfall, droughts and floods in both countries.

To meet these, both countries have set up national parks, sanctuaries and biosphere reserves, passed environmental protection laws, and are promoting afforestation and non-conventional sources of energy.
